Waste kings

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
from picking through rubbish bins and scavenging on landfills, waste pickers are saving municipalities millions of rands every year.

Summary:
South Africa has between 60 000 to 90 000 waste pickers who work tirelessly on the streets, picking recyclable waste material from rubbish bins in suburbs and scavenging on landfills to find paper, cupboards, steel and plastic and in a recent surprise finding, these invisible workers, are saving our municipalities up to R750-million a year.

According to a report by the Centre for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR),waste pickers divert recyclables away from the landfills at no, or little cost, by recovering around 80 to 90% of waste. It is estimated that each waste picker diverts up to 24 tons of packaging waste every year and they do this while pulling their heavy trolleys around 40 kilometres per day from the suburbs to the landfills and back again.

But the waste and recycling sector is on the brink of change thanks to mandatory extended producer responsibility, which means producers (of end waste material) will now be responsible for the waste they generate, cutting informal waste pickers out, and without any real means to earn a living from these recyclables.

The CSIR has done research to see if waste pickers can be incorporated into the formal economy, and Professor Linda Godfrey, who led the study, said: "The most surprising finding for me was when we started to attach financial values to the savings by municipalities as a result of informal waste pickers."


Further information:
There are two main types of waste pickers

1. landfill pickers who work under the worst conditions but for the highest returns. A landfill worker can earn a minimum of around R500 a day and some usually decide to live on the landfill to collect as much recyclable waste as possible.

2. Street pickers are the ones we see mostly on the streets pulling or riding their trolleys through the suburbs. They usually scavenge the rubbish bins from business or apartment complexes and homes looking for any recyclables. On "rubbish collections day" they usually walk around 40 kilometres from their homes to the neighborhoods and will pick through the bins before the municipal trucks arrive. Once they have a load of about 14 -25 kilograms, they head back to the middlemen or buy-back centres where they sell their load for as little as R1.50p\kg. So street pickers can expect to make around R120 a day for their loads.

In this insert will speak to the key role players in the waste picking industry including Nkosinathi Ndhlovu, a former contract worker who used to earn around R120 a day as a casual worker, then five years ago he decided to join the landfill pickers at one of South Africa's biggest landfill - Robinson Deep in Johannesburg.

He says when he started waste picking, he used to live at home in Soweto and he used to take the train to get him to town and he found he would sometimes arrive very late to start picking, so he would sleep at the landfill with a few other waste pickers. He would spend a few nights there at a time before he went down to sell what he had collected. Nowadays he lives in a flat a few kilometres from the landfill with his children.

He says that on the landfill, the 100 or so guys work independently but they help each other by forming almost a stokvel where in the event where one of them has a family member that passes away, each one contributes R100 and that is given to the waste picker to help with burial finances. In the event that a waste picker passes away, they each contribute R200 to give to his family.
Most waste pickers are family bread winners and in the event of their death, their family is asked to provide a young person to replace the deceased on the landfill.

Nkosinathi also runs his own recycling business by collecting plastic clothing hangers from the landfill and reselling them to his own clients – mainly the Chinese in town, who export the recycled plastic back to China where it is made into bio-diesel.
From his initial idea he now has three other waste picker who help him sort the hangers while he is picking from the landfill. He targets around a ton to two tons of the plastic hangers and from reselling them to his Chinese clients, he can pay the waste pickers who help him sort the hangers. He also has his own bakkies to make deliveries as well as to pick up old hangers from his suppliers.


We will also meet Sifiso Ngobese, a social entrepreneur who has designed and made newer models of trolleys which are far more visible especially in the dark and which provide space for Big corporates to advertise on the trolleys. He has already run campaigns with both Nedbank and Redbull. The money made from the advertising is then shared with the waste pickers.

Simon Mbata is a waste picker and the Chairperson of the Waste Pickers Association.

Press Release:


Waste Kings
It’s arguably one of the filthiest jobs one could take on - picking through dustbins to eke out a meagre existence. But the informal waste pickers who fan out across suburbia and recycle what’s thrown away by South Africans - over 100 million tonnes of trash every year - are saving municipalities millions of rands. Carte Blanche meets the people picking up after the nation.


Script:


Script

VO: It’s another early start to the day and a long walk awaits Thulani Sokhela as he heads out with his constant companion – his trolley.
UPSOUND Thulani Sokhela TCR: 03:56:00:
You see where I get my materials, its from homes...households, you can go door to door.
VO: South Africa generates approximately 108 million tonnes of waste every year.

From rotten food and medical waste to plastic, the landfills are filling up fast but just ten percent of this waste gets recycled – mostly by waste pickers.
LINK TCR: 05:11:09:06 It is one of the dirtiest jobs you can imagine, trawling through rubbish dumps and bins; trying to find recyclable goods just so you can earn a few hundred Rands… [cut link]
UPSOUND TCR: 00:01:00:24 Prof Linda Godfrey: …Waste pickers especially, in South Africa as in most developed countries, are informal sector collectors that earn a livelihood through the recovery of recyclable waste ….
VO: It’s estimated that there are between 60 to 90 thousand waste pickers around the country and many of them are often seen pushing and pulling heavy trolleys on the streets.

Thulani Sokhela is a father of four. Five years ago, he lost his job as a call centre agent and became a waste picker, rummaging through dustbins on the leafy suburbs in Roodepoort in Gauteng.
UPSOUND Thulani TCR: 03:52:02:14…. there was a program called Collect-A-Can and that’s what inspired me. I started collecting cans until I could see that there was a bit of money coming in.
LINK: Waste pickers recover almost 90 percent of all paper and packaging waste that would otherwise end up in landfills. In fact it is estimated that each waste picker collects up to 24 tonnes of waste every year.
VO: Professor Linda Godfrey is the Principal Scientist at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research. She’s done extensive studies on South Africa’s informal waste recycling sector.
UPSOUND TCR: 00:03:18:21 Prof Godfrey: ...because they can’t find any other livelihood they go onto landfill site or they move to curb site to collect recyclable material because there’s value in our recyclable waste that we put out.
LINK TCR: 06:00:03:23
It’s on cold winter mornings like this one where most of us are still in the comfort of our homes, but we forget there are waste pickers that are out in the streets as early as 3am digging through our rubbish bins and landfills...searching for recyclable goods to sell, to eke out a meagre living.
UPSOUND TCR: 03:58:23 Thulani:
Back when I started, I used to wake up around 4am. I had to wake up and walk a distance like 5 kilometres to Roodepoort where white people put out their dustbins outside.
UPSOUND [TCR: 20:17:56:07] Simon Mbata: …for trolley pushers it’s a difficult thing because they woke up early, they have to be in the front, before the municipal trucks can come and collects.
VO: Simon Mbata is the chairperson of the South African Waste Pickers Association. Seventeen years ago, he left his job as a part-time contract worker to become a waste picker.
UPSOUND [TCR: 20:15:25:04] Simon: …contract jobs don’t pay. Contract jobs you work for certain periods and you are unemployed again … so here I found the opportunity where one can make a living…
LINK TCR: 06:06:48:04
Cardboard, glass bottles and plastic bags these are just some of the recyclable waste materials that South Africans are throwing away every day.
VO: And with just over 1300 landfills across the country, these items are taking up valuable space and decreasing landfill capacity.
Waste pickers aren’t just cleaning up the streets, they also have a direct impact on the environment and the public purse.
UPSOUND [TCR: 01:09:58:11] Simon: …one benefit of the waste pickers is for municipalities, the amount and the volumes of waste that is being collected by those trolley pushers was supposed to be transported by the municipality to the landfill...
UPSOUND TCR: 00:15:10:18 Prof Godfrey:……………
The informal waste sector is actually saving municipalities; we estimate somewhere between R300 and R750 million a year in terms of landfill air space savings.
VO: But for waste pickers like Thulani, helping municipalities is not his end goal - there’s money to be made from every day rubbish.
UPSOUND TCR: 03:47:04:10 Thulani:
Per week, if I’ve worked well I can make something like R1000 and something, maybe R2000
UPSOUND TCR: 10:21:07:02 Michella Hatting:
… we have nine branches, across the whole group 30% of the material that we receive, comes from the informal sector.
VO: Remade Recycling is the largest trader of recyclable material in the country, and spends millions each year, buying material from waste pickers.
UPSOUND TCR: 10:28:54:00 Michella Hatting:
What we spend on the waste pickers obviously depends very much on the tonnages that they bring in... but if we look at a branch like the newtown branch, , 43% of the material that we buy, comes from your waste pickers
VO: And for a waste picker to keep making money, they need to take care of their most important possession - their trolley.
UPSOUND TCR: 03:59:35:10 Thulani:
This trolley can take something like a hundred to 200 kilograms It’s very strong.
UPSOUND TCR: 10:22:08 Sifiso Ngobese
... most of these guys get involved in accidents, they pull these ragged trolleys, you can’t even identify them on the road...
VO: Sifiso Ngobese is a social entrepreneur. Several years ago, he quit his well-paying corporate job to find ways to help waste pickers on the streets by designing better trolleys.
UPSOUND TCR: 10:22:08 Sifiso Ngobese
... our trolleys are much more safe, they’ve got reflective material so they enhanced visibility and the clothes that we give them as well. They get the trolley and the gear free of charge.
UPSOUND TCR: 02:20:35:00 Sifiso Ngobese
Our vision is to give the informal waste pickers of South Africa dignity, so that when you see them on the road first of all, you’re not seen as a nuisance.
VO: Thulani has fitted his trolley with a number plate to help identify it when it’s stolen. He says taxi drivers are also a big problem.
UPSOUND TCR: 04:02:04 Thulani:
...because they don’t tolerate us. When you walking they hoot but where must I go, must I fly with this thing?
UPSOUND TCR: 00:33:33:13 Prof Godfrey:
I don’t think that being waste picker is the greatest livelihood...
Waste material attracts rodents, parasites, all kinds of potential pathogens that might be in that waste as well that they’re exposed to.
VO: But at the end of the day, Thulani returns home with enough money to feed his family for another day…

15 Seconds

1.) South Africa generates approximately 108 million tonnes of waste every year, but only 10 percent of that gets recycled mostly by surbanan waste pickers.
UPSOUND TCR: 00:08:18:11 Linda Godfrey
..In fact you and I as households are actually quite bad at separating our recyclable material and actually contributing to a recycling economy.

2.) It’s one of the dirtiest jobs in the world, picking through rubbish dumps for a small income. How are suburban waste pickers saving municipalities up to R750 million every year? [10’]

3.) South Africa is fast running out of landfill space and only ten percent of all waste generated ends being recycled.
UPSOUND TCR: 00:15:10:18 Prof Godfrey: “The informal waste sector is actually saving municipalities; we estimate somewhere between R300 and R750 million a year in terms of landfill air space savings.”
10 Second\In studio
It’s one of the worst jobs you can think of – picking through bins and rubbish dumps - just to earn a living. But suburban waste pickers are saving municipalities millions of Rands every year.

Street pickers are the ones we see mostly on the streets pulling or riding their trolleys through the suburbs. They usually scavenge the rubbish bins from business or apartment complexes and homes looking for any recyclables. On "rubbish collections day" they usually walk around 40 kilometres from their homes to the neighborhoods and will pick through the bins before the municipal trucks arrive. Once they have a load of about 14 -25 kilograms, they head back to the middlemen or buy-back centres where they sell their load for as little as R1.50p\kg. So street pickers can expect to make around R120 a day for their loads. In this insert will speak to the key role players in the waste picking industry including Nkosinathi Ndhlovu, a former contract worker who used to earn around R120 a day as a casual worker, then five years ago he decided to join the landfill pickers at one of South Africa's biggest landfill - Robinson Deep in Johannesburg. He says when he started waste picking, he used to live at home in Soweto and he used to take the train to get him to town and he found he would sometimes arrive very late to start picking, so he would sleep at the landfill with a few other waste pickers. He would spend a few nights there at a time before he went down to sell what he had collected. Nowadays he lives in a flat a few kilometres from the landfill with his children. He says that on the landfill, the 100 or so guys work independently but they help each other by forming almost a stokvel where in the event where one of them has a family member that passes away, each one contributes R100 and that is given to the waste picker to help with burial finances. In the event that a waste picker passes away, they each contribute R200 to give to his family. Most waste pickers are family bread winners and in the event of their death, their family is asked to provide a young person to replace the deceased on the landfill. Nkosinathi also runs his own recycling business by collecting plastic clothing hangers from the landfill and reselling them to his own clients – mainly the Chinese in town, who export the recycled plastic back to China where it is made into bio-diesel. From his initial idea he now has three other waste picker who help him sort the hangers while he is picking from the landfill. He targets around a ton to two tons of the plastic hangers and from reselling them to his Chinese clients, he can pay the waste pickers who help him sort the hangers. He also has his own bakkies to make deliveries as well as to pick up old hangers from his suppliers. We will also meet Sifiso Ngobese, a social entrepreneur who has designed and made newer models of trolleys which are far more visible especially in the dark and which provide space for Big corporates to advertise on the trolleys. He has already run campaigns with both Nedbank and Redbull. The money made from the advertising is then shared with the waste pickers. Simon Mbata is a waste picker and the Chairperson of the Waste Pickers Association.
